topComments.author: TacticalCoder
topComments.text: 0/1 Knapsack is a wonderful little problem, especially with its dynamic programming solution. Now I may be mistaken but when I learned about 0/1 Knapsack three decades ago, my immediate thought was that for quite some cases you could do, using dynamic programming, an approximate version (requiring less memory and hence well, for example fitting into memory) and prove that your solution was "at most 1% off of the optimal solution" . Never really looked into it though so I may have be wrong. Basically say you need to 0/1 Knapsack the quantities 1739, 2989, 3798 and 4233, etc.: you can e.g. divide them by 10 and then round them up, so you've now got 174, 299, 380 and 424 and you need much less memory to run your dynamic programming solution to 0/1 Knapsack. And the best solution you find is guaranteed to be at most x% off the optimal solution. Something like that. Does that work? Anyone ever heard about something similar?

topComments.author: shoo
topComments.text: I was curious about the issue the author called out with the baseline knapsack algorithm -- that it was running out of memory. It looks like pytorch's various knapsack implementations (including the one contributed by the author) are here: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/31ba9a56657bc887c957... appears to be used e.g. here https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/31ba9a56657bc887c957... One thing that jumps out at me while staring at the baseline dp_knapsack code is that it isn't very clear what the units used to measure memory are meant to be. The dp_knapsack code assumes that memory & max_memory (aka the memory budget) are floats. dp_knapsack internally multiplies these floating-point memory values by 10,000 & then rounds them to integers to quantise the memory values -- the quantised max_memory value defines the size of one dimension of the dynamic programming table. the other dimension is sized by the item count. From reading patches of partitioners.py, it seems like the memory budget is meant to be a floating point number between 0.0 & 1.0, and presumably the memory of each item is normalised relative to that memory budget? If so, & dp_knapsack is called with a max_memory of 1.0, then the a 2d array for n items is allocated and m=10,000 quantised memory values is allocated as shape (n+1, m+1). So for 100 items that'd be an array of shape (101, 10001) - it's filled with float32s, so 4 bytes per element, so the size required for the table would be ... about 4MB. So it's not obvious why that would be running out of memory. Another possible explanation of why the baseline dp knapsack could be using a bunch of memory -- speculation -- is that some code could be calling dp_knapsack with a different unit convention than what dp_knapsack expects --- suppose a caller passes in memory & max_memory values that are measured in floating-point GB. If the max_memory was passed in as 1024.0 then, for 100 items, the dp_knapsack code would allocate a float32 array of shape (101, 10240001) and this would require about 4GB. Given the units of these inputs aren't documented (& certainly not enforced by the type system) & there aren't runtime range checks on the value of max_memory there's a lot of room for something like this to be happening. Perhaps dp_knapsack could be reimplemented where it is responsible for rescaling input memory values relative to max_memory, where the rescaling always forces max_memory to be 1 before the memory values are quantised. Then there wouldn't be a way for the caller to get the undocumented calling convention wrong.

jobs.text: I’m Chris, VP Engineering at Fazeshift. We’re nine engineers plus our Founder/CTO and me, and I’m hiring someone who can help us do more, better: increase both what we can build and the quality and sophistication of the software we build. Accounts receivable sounds boring until you look under the hood. It sits at the intersection of money, business relationships, software systems of various vintages, and a huge amount of repetitive human work. Instead of giving finance teams another dashboard to stare at, we’re building AI agents that actually do the work across billing, collections, payments, cash application, and the systems connecting them. We’ve grown revenue 12x since 2024, and eight unicorns now run AR on Fazeshift. A big part of what makes the engineering interesting is that we’re intentionally not the system of record. Our customers already run on ERPs, CRMs, banks, billing systems, payment processors, spreadsheets, and internal software, so we have to understand state across systems we don’t control, act safely in them, and recover when reality disagrees with what an API says should have happened. A timeout doesn’t necessarily mean a write failed. Webhooks can arrive late or twice. A payment may not contain enough information to identify an invoice. In those cases, blindly retrying can be exactly the wrong thing to do. We use coding agents heavily ourselves. Engineers use Conductor, stacked PRs, Linear, and multiple frontier models every day, with internal skills and tooling that let agents drive and validate our local development environment. We’re especially interested in engineers whose development workflow has already materially changed because of coding agents: people who are comfortable delegating meaningful work, keeping independent threads moving in parallel, debugging where agents get stuck, and improving the surrounding system when the workflow breaks down. But generated code is still your code . Judgment, debugging, systems thinking, taste, and understanding what actually shipped matter more here, not less. Our development style is roughly: design enough to find the shape of the problem, then build to learn. There’s a short distance here between noticing a problem, deciding what should happen, building it, and seeing the result in production with our customers. You’ll own meaningful problems from ambiguity through design, implementation, rollout, and production, and you’ll work directly with the people affected by what you build. We’re looking for 5+ years of professional experience, strong TypeScript/full-stack skills, solid systems judgment, and real production ownership. No fintech background needed. Stack: TypeScript/Next.js, tRPC, Prisma/MySQL/PlanetScale, Inngest, AWS. I read every HN application myself. quantaArticles.author: Robin George Andrews

quantaArticles.title: Is ‘Attention’ the Essence of Intelligence?

quantaArticles.title: How Does Life Unfold? A Landscape Metaphor Comes Into Its Own.
quantaArticles.description: C.H. Waddington’s powerful image of embryonic stem cells specializing on a rolling landscape has captivated biologists since the 1950s. Experimental data is finally confirming, and complicating, his visionary ideas.
quantaArticles.author: Philip Ball

infoqArticles.title: Reverse Engineer Anything Project Brings AI Agents to Binary Analysis
infoqArticles.description: Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is an open-source project with over 200K GitHub stars that connects coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex to reverse-engineering tools like Ghidra, Hopper, and IDA. The project lets developers inspect compiled binaries, trace function calls, and investigate how applications implement specific features. By Renato Losio
infoqArticles.author: Renato Losio

infoqArticles.title: Amazon Acquires DuckLabs and Integrates DuckDB in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL
infoqArticles.description: Amazon has acquired DuckLabs, the company behind the analytical database DuckDB. Co-founders Hannes Mühleisen and Mark Raasveldt will continue to lead the team under AWS. The acquisition aims to enhance the development and reach of DuckDB while maintaining its open-source status. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL gets its first DuckDB-powered feature following the acquisition. By Gianmarco Nalin
infoqArticles.author: Gianmarco Nalin

infoqArticles.title: Google EnvHarness Enables Self-Evolving Agents to Learn in Dynamics Environments
infoqArticles.description: Google researchers open sourced EnvHarness, a framework that dynamically adapts agent-training environments to an agent's weaknesses without modifying the agent, environment, or evaluation system. According to the researchers, this approach can improve both learning effectiveness and efficiency while helping agents overcome their weaknesses. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: Zod Brings In-Process Schema Compilation and a 9x Cut in Memory Footprint
infoqArticles.description: Zod is a TypeScript-focused schema validation library that recently released versions 4.5 and 4.6. Key updates include schema compilation for faster data parsing, significant memory usage reductions, and new validation features. The library supports efficient validation processes and remains popular in the JavaScript ecosystem, achieving millions of downloads weekly. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: Uber Automates Dependency Analysis Across Its Service Mesh
infoqArticles.description: Uber has developed an automated dependency analysis system that uses RPC middleware and production metrics to correlate caller and downstream failures. The approach classifies dependencies as fail-close, fail-open, or unknown and addresses limitations of sampled distributed tracing for rare failures across Uber’s large service mesh. By Leela Kumili
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: AI in Production: Panellists Highlight Silent Failures, Harness Engineering, and Agent Governance
infoqArticles.description: A recent InfoQ webinar examined operational challenges in deploying agentic systems. Key points included issues like semantic and embedding drift, which can lead to significant errors. Experts discussed the need for automated code reviews, continuous evaluation of models, and enhanced privacy measures. The session emphasised a strategic approach to deployment and security management. By Olimpiu Po
infoqArticles.author: Olimpiu Pop

infoqArticles.title: Grafana Applies SLOs and Error Budgets to AI Agent Behaviour
infoqArticles.description: Grafana Labs is proposing a familiar reliability engineering approach for one of the less familiar problems in modern software: how to measure whether an AI agent is actually behaving well. By Craig Risi
infoqArticles.author: Craig Risi

infoqArticles.title: Mini book: Evolutionary Architecture in Practice
infoqArticles.description: Discover how to keep software evolvable as systems, technology, and teams shift. This edition explores agentic fitness functions for semantic drift, treating human comprehension as a core design metric, cross-cloud guardrails for regional autonomy, and aligning technical boundaries with Conway’s Law. Move beyond static diagrams to continuous feedback systems that keep change safe and intentional.
infoqArticles.author: InfoQ

infoqArticles.title: Helidon 27 Introduces Restructured Programming Models and New Messaging and Data Modules
infoqArticles.description: The release of Helidon 27 is the first release that follows the Oracle Tip & Tail Model of Library Development by which the Tip adopts the latest Java technology while the Tail provides a more stable and secure baseline. Concurrent with the release of JDK 27, new features in Helidon 27 include: an introduction to new major modules, Helidon Messaging and Helidon Data JDBC. By Michael Redlich
infoqArticles.author: Michael Redlich

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: Exploding GPUs
infoqArticles.description: Andrew Martin discusses why AI security is fundamentally tied to Kubernetes security. He shares insights into the evolving AI threat landscape, covering non-deterministic agent behavior, GPU supply chain vulnerabilities, shared compute risks, and practical defense strategies - from prompt firewalling to agentic identity - to help secure cloud-native AI workloads in production environments. By Andr
infoqArticles.author: Andrew Martin

infoqArticles.title: AWS Introduces Strands Decider 2B and Strands Box for AI Agent Development
infoqArticles.description: AWS has introduced two open-source projects for AI agent development: Strands Decider 2B, a small model designed to make decisions within agent workflows, and Strands Box, a sandbox for controlling agent execution. Both projects address different aspects of building agents that use tools, execute code, and interact with external systems. By Daniel Dominguez
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Dominguez

infoqArticles.title: Article: Cryptographic Foundation of Mobile ID Systems: An ISO/IEC 18013-5 Enterprise Architecture Blueprint
infoqArticles.description: This article provides a framework for asking the right architectural questions before an enterprise commits to an mDL provider or library. It shows which components can be abstracted safely, which trust boundaries must remain visible to the enterprise, what cryptographic and interoperability properties should be verified, and how requirements change across real-world use cases. By Praveen Kumar Go
infoqArticles.author: Praveen Kumar Gopalakrishnan

infoqArticles.title: Chainguard Launches Secure Workspaces and Checks for AI Coding Agents
infoqArticles.description: Software supply chain security company Chainguard has announced two beta products for running and testing code written by developers and AI agents. Chainguard Workspaces provides remote development environments based on hardened microVMs, while Chainguard Checks moves continuous integration into the development loop. The company announced both products at its Assemble London event. By Matt Saunder
infoqArticles.author: Matt Saunders

infoqArticles.title: Microsoft Commits Maia to Multi-Gigawatt Inference, and Its Efficiency Metric Draws Questions
infoqArticles.description: Microsoft will scale its Maia accelerator family to multi-gigawatt deployments from 2027, making it the primary inference system for its own products. Maia 300 collapses scale-up and scale-out onto one Ethernet fabric and moves KV state between prefill and decode workers without leaving it. Practitioners have questioned the tokens-per-watt claim that leads the announcement. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
infoqArticles.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers

infoqArticles.title: Instagram Modernized its UI with an AI-Native Architecture, Cutting Token Costs by 33%
infoqArticles.description: Instagram Direct migrated its Android UI from the legacy Android View system to Jetpack Compose, creating an AI-native UI codebase that is easier for AI coding agents to understand, modify, and maintain. According to Instagram engineers, the migration reduced UI code volume by 50% and token costs per AI agent session by 33%. By Sergio De Simone
